title: Animation Basics
summary: Learn the foundations of animation: types of animation, frames, timing and spacing, the twelve principles, the production pipeline from script to animatic to final edit, free and professional tools, and building a demo reel and career. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Beginners, art students, illustrators and creators interested in 2D, 3D or stop-motion animation

body.p: Animation creates the illusion of movement by showing a sequence of still images quickly. Because the eye holds each image for a fraction of a second, images shown at about 12 or more per second blend into smooth motion. Animation is used in films, series, adverts, games, music videos, education and explainer videos.

list: 2D hand-drawn or digital frame-by-frame animation: each frame is drawn.
2D rigged or cut-out animation: characters are built from parts that are moved, saving time.
3D computer animation: models are built, rigged and animated in 3D software.
Stop motion: real objects such as clay figures or paper are photographed a frame at a time.
Motion graphics: animated text, shapes and infographics for adverts and explainers.

body.p: African animation is growing, with studios in Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Ghana, Egypt and elsewhere creating series and films rooted in African stories, languages and mythologies.

body.tip: Watch animation frame by frame (many video players allow this) to see how motion is built.

body.p: Film animation commonly runs at 24 frames per second (fps). A 10-second shot needs 24 x 10 = 240 frames. Animating "on twos", where each drawing is held for two frames, needs 120 drawings for the same shot, which is common in 2D animation and saves a lot of work. Each minute at 24 fps is 24 x 60 = 1440 frames, so a 90-minute feature contains 90 x 1440 = 129 600 frames.

list: Key poses (keys) show the most important positions of an action.
Breakdowns show how the movement travels between keys.
In-betweens fill the remaining frames to make motion smooth.

body.p: Timing is how many frames an action takes: more frames make it slower, fewer make it faster. Spacing is how far an object moves between frames: drawings close together look slow, far apart look fast. A heavy object starts and stops slowly; a light one changes speed quickly.

body.tip: Act out the movement yourself and time it with a stopwatch before animating.

body.p: Animators widely use a set of twelve principles, popularised by Disney animators Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, to make movement believable and appealing.

list: Squash and stretch: objects deform to show weight and flexibility, like a bouncing ball.
Anticipation: a small movement prepares for a big one, such as crouching before a jump.
Staging: present an idea clearly so the audience knows where to look.
Straight-ahead action and pose-to-pose: two ways of working through a scene.
Follow-through and overlapping action: parts such as hair and clothing keep moving after the body stops.
Slow in and slow out (easing): more frames near the start and end of a movement.
Arcs: most natural movements follow curved paths.
Secondary action: smaller actions that support the main one.
Timing, exaggeration, solid drawing and appeal complete the set.

body.tip: Animate a bouncing ball first; it teaches timing, spacing, arcs and squash and stretch in one exercise.

steps: Concept and script: the idea, story and dialogue.
Design: characters, props and backgrounds, with a consistent style.
Storyboard: drawings of each shot showing composition and action, like a comic strip.
Animatic: the storyboard timed to a temporary soundtrack to test pacing.
Voice recording, usually done before animation so mouths can match the dialogue.
Animation: layout, key poses, in-betweens and clean-up.
Sound design, music and final edit.

body.p: A 30-second advert at 12 drawings per second could need 12 x 30 = 360 drawings, which is why careful planning in the storyboard and animatic stages saves weeks of work. On team projects, a shared schedule and clear file naming keep everyone working on the right version.

body.tip: Never skip the animatic: fixing timing problems there is far cheaper than after animation.

list: 2D: Krita, OpenToonz and Pencil2D are free; Toon Boom Harmony and Adobe Animate are industry tools; phone and tablet apps such as FlipaClip are good for practice.
3D: Blender is free and powerful for modelling, rigging, animation and rendering; Maya is widely used in studios.
Motion graphics: Adobe After Effects and free alternatives.
Stop motion: phone apps with onion skinning and a stable tripod.

body.p: A drawing tablet greatly improves 2D work. 3D rendering needs a capable computer, but many learners start on modest machines and render at low resolution while practising.

Onion skinning shows faint versions of the previous and next frames, helping you judge spacing and keep drawings consistent. A short movement of half a second at 25 fps covers about 12.5 frames, so onion skins help make each one flow.

body.tip: Learn one tool well rather than many superficially; animation principles transfer between programs.

body.p: Animation careers include animator, storyboard artist, character designer, background artist, rigger, 3D modeller, compositor, motion designer and director. Studios, advertising agencies, game developers and education companies hire animators, and many work as freelancers for international clients.

list: Build a demo reel of 30 to 90 seconds showing your best work first.
Show a range: walk cycles, lip sync, acting shots and short complete pieces.
Share work-in-progress online, join animation communities and take part in challenges and festivals.
Learn to take feedback and revise quickly; animation is a collaborative craft.
Agree on deliverables, revisions and payment in writing with clients.

body.p: Stories from your own culture, language and experience can make your work stand out in a global market looking for fresh voices.

body.tip: Finish small projects: a complete 10-second piece is more impressive than an unfinished epic.
